newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank rejects Bonn plan to revalue gold.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank rejects Bonn plan to revalue gold.

text.p: The German Bundesbank on Thursday issued a strong statement rejecting Bonn government plans to revalue its assets and demand an immediate payout of the profit booked from these hidden reserves.
But the government coalition said it was going to stick with its plans.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel two weeks ago announced plans to revalue the central bank's assets to give a much-needed injection of cash to Bonn's strapped public finances.
The central bank warned that this plan ran the risk of undermining the stability of the European single currency.

In its statement, the Bundesbank said the Bonn concept was not in line with rules planned for changes to central bank accounting after the move to a single currency as it linked the revaluation to an immediate payout of the unrealised profit.
This payout should normally only be made at the time of entry to the single European currency, it said.

"A payout of hidden reserves would be controllable in monetary policy terms depending on its size. But if it is legally enforced this would mean an intervention in the Bundesbank's monetary policy," the Bundesbank said.
"Such a measure would be in contradiction with the German tradition and with the Maastricht Treaty's view on the independence of the central banks."
The central bank said the plan foresaw a markedly higher value for Bundesbank reserves and a payout of the resultant profit in both 1997 and 1998.

Such a payout could only make a limited contribution to improving Bonn's finances in the long-term, the Bundesbank said. It would not contribute to a formal fulfilment of the criteria in line with the Maastricht treaty.
The Maastricht Treaty calls for central banks to meet certain targets on fiscal deficits. Germany is having tremendous problems in cutting back its deficit far enough to reach these goals.

The parliamentary group leaders from Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and the Free Democrats (FDP) said in a statement: "The coalition will strive to include the revaluation of the reserves into the current legislative process."
In a two-page statement the coalition said the stability and independence of the Bundesbank will not be affected by the revalution plans.

"The successful stability policies of the Bundesbank as well as its sole monetary political responsiblity will not in any way be hampered by the planned adjustments of the currency reserves," the statement said.
The statement added that the plans to revalue the reserves was not an attack on the independence of the central bank.

"The financial solidity of the Bundesbank will be completely protected through the cautious revaluation," the coalition said. "Even today the gold reserves in most European central banks are already valued much higher than they are at the Bundesbank."
